candidates.attacker_control: Full control of the serialized byte stream: any party able to supply a CAS file/stream/URL that an application feeds to CasIOUtils.load (e.g., opening a downloaded/user-supplied CAS in the CAS Editor, CVD, or any app using the public load(URL,...)/load(InputStream,...) APIs), or able to replace/point at such data; and any client able to open a connection to a deployed Vinci binary Analysis Engine service port (jVinci BaseServer accepts frames with no authentication/authorization), or a malicious service that answers a binary-mode client stub. The first bytes of the input decide which deserialization branch is taken, and the header flags decide whether readObject is invoked.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: (1) XML CAS paths (XCAS/XMI) are parsed through hardened factories (XMLUtils: disallow-doctype, load-external-dtd=false, XInclude off) and do not reach readObject(); the risk is confined to the Java-serialized/embedded-TSI branches. (2) The Java-serialized CAS forms are documented/legacy formats, so this can be argued as by-design; however CasIOUtils.load chooses the branch automatically from unauthenticated bytes and offers URL/stream overloads, so callers cannot enforce trust by construction, and no filter/allowlist exists anywhere (grep for ObjectInputFilter/serialFilter returned nothing). (3) The default Vinci service script launches the XCAS variant, not the binary one, so the remote path requires the binary service/stub to be used; but that variant is shipped, has a main(), and jVinci performs no authentication. (4) I checked for later-added mitigations (filters, readOnly deserialization options) and found none in this snapshot. (5) I did not execute anything or verify gadget availability/exploitability at runtime.
candidates.impact: Deserialization of untrusted data in a widely used framework's core loading path and in its network transport: attacker-controlled byte streams cause arbitrary object graphs to be instantiated inside the target JVM, which is the classic precondition for remote code execution via gadget chains, plus denial of service (memory/CPU) and unauthorized replacement of the CAS type system/index definition (data integrity) through the CASCompleteSerializer/CASMgrSerializer paths. In the Vinci case the boundary is remote and unauthenticated; in the CAS-file case the boundary is any untrusted CAS/TSI artifact a user or service loads.
candidates.prerequisites: One of: (1) an application/deployment loads CAS or TSI data from a source not known to be trusted (file share, upload, URL, message), which is exactly what the auto-detecting load API is for; or (2) the opt-in Vinci binary service variant (VinciBinaryAnalysisEngineService_impl, e.g., selected via service deployment/binary stub) is deployed and network-reachable. For code-execution impact, a deserialization gadget chain must exist on the target JVM's classpath; otherwise the observed impact is at least object-injection/DoS and type-system replacement before any validation.
candidates.root_cause: Java object deserialization is applied directly to attacker-influenced bytes with no ObjectInputFilter, class allowlist, or format authentication: (a) CasIOUtils.load() auto-detects the input format from the first 9 bytes and, if the data is neither XML nor a recognized binary header, constructs a new ObjectInputStream and calls readObject(); (b) binary CAS headers that set the typeSystemIncluded/typeSystemIndexDefIncluded flags cause BinaryCasSerDes.maybeReadEmbeddedTSI() to wrap the attacker's stream in an ObjectInputStream and call readObject() (and CasIOUtils.readCasManager() does the same for an externally supplied TSI stream); (c) SerializationUtils.deserialize() is a generic ObjectInputStream.readObject() wrapper that the Vinci binary AE transport invokes on network frames (the server deserializes request 'BinaryCAS' bytes; the client stub deserializes response bytes). No source file in the snapshot contains an ObjectInputFilter or equivalent guard.
candidates.title: Unfiltered Java deserialization of attacker-controlled CAS/binary data (CAS load APIs and Vinci binary transport)
candidates.trace: Network/file input -> CasIOUtils.load(URL/InputStream, CAS) [CasIOUtils.java:214-247, 284-380] reads first 9 bytes; not XML and not CommonSerDes binary header -> 'Java Object loading' ObjectInputStream.readObject() [CasIOUtils.java:461-466]. Alternatively a valid binary CAS header with TS/TSI flags -> BinaryCasSerDes.reinit -> maybeReadEmbeddedTSI -> new ObjectInputStream(dis).readObject() [BinaryCasSerDes.java:617-629]; separately supplied TSI stream -> CasIOUtils.readCasManager -> readObject [CasIOUtils.java:595-605]. Independently, a Vinci binary request reaches VinciBinaryAnalysisEngineService_impl.eval -> analyze -> aRequestFrame.fgetTrueBinary("BinaryCAS") -> SerializationUtils.deserialize -> ObjectInputStream.readObject [VinciBinaryAnalysisEngineService_impl.java:201-211; SerializationUtils.java:79-88]; the stub performs the same on response bytes [VinciBinaryAnalysisEngineServiceStub.java:263-269]. The returned object is only cast afterwards (e.g., to CASCompleteSerializer/CASMgrSerializer), so gadget-chain side effects occur during readObject(), before any type/format validation.
candidates.unverified: Runtime exploitability is not verified: no payload was built, no gadget chain was confirmed on a typical UIMA classpath, and no deployment was tested. Whether a specific application feeds untrusted CAS files/streams to CasIOUtils.load, or deploys the Vinci binary service, is deployment-dependent. The exact upstream fix (if any) is unknown; impact severity may be judged lower if all CAS/TSI inputs are considered trusted.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data (secondary: CWE-20 Improper Input Validation)

coverage_summary: Scope reviewed: all 1,860 model-visible files were considered via directory listing and targeted searches; the P1 relation index covered 1,810 files (50 missing, 1 parse error) and provides only syntax-level relations (no control/data flow, no reachability, no runtime proof), so every indexed hint used in this review was verified against source text. Deep inspection focused on: jVinci transport (frame parsing, BaseServer/BaseClient, XTalk, VNS), uimaj-adapter-vinci (binary/X CAS service + stub), uimaj-core CAS serialization (CasIOUtils, BinaryCasSerDes, SerializationUtils, SerialFormat, XMLUtils, CasIOUtils URL APIs), uimaj-core PEAR tooling (InstallationController, FileUtil, PackageInstaller/PackageCreator, XMLUtil/ProcessUtil), uimaj-cpe (CPMEngine/DebugControlThread, VinciCasProcessorDeployer, sockets, Checkpoint), uimaj-tools (CVD, doc analyzer, annotation view HTML/XSLT, PEAR installer/merger), jcasgen/PearPackaging Maven plugins, and the bootstrap/migration utilities. Cross-cutting searches were run for command execution, SQL, reflection, XML parser construction, archive extraction, URL connections, cryptography/randomness, temp files, and Java serialization. Test sources/resources are not part of the visible snapshot, so no tests were available to corroborate intended trust boundaries.
limitations: Not all 1,860 files were read line-by-line; coverage was search- and module-prioritized, so a narrower issue in an uninspected file cannot be excluded.

The relation index is partial (1,810/1,860 files, 1 parse error) and explicitly lacks data-flow, control-flow, semantic resolution and reachability, so no index edge was treated as proof; all cited behavior was confirmed in source.

No code was executed, no dependencies/classpath were inspected, and no gadget-chain feasibility was verified; the RCE impact of the candidate is therefore a well-established consequence class, not a demonstrated exploit.

No runtime deployment knowledge: whether a given installation loads untrusted CAS/TSI data or runs the Vinci binary service is environment-specific; the Java-serialized CAS formats may be considered a legacy/by-design feature by the project.
The exact configuration of upstream security fixes is unknown (no patches, advisories, or history available in this run), so severity and which sink would be fixed upstream remain uncertain.

Alternative plausible but unselected issues (PEAR Zip Slip, jVinci parser DoS, opt-in doctype property, descriptor-driven command construction, predictable temp dir) are recorded as rejected leads and were not fully traced to a concrete end-to-end attack.

rejected_leads.lead: Zip Slip / path traversal in PEAR-JAR extraction: FileUtil.extractFilesFromJar writes new File(targetDir, jarEntry.getName()) then opens FileOutputStream with no canonical-path containment check (uimaj-core/src/main/java/org/apache/uima/pear/util/FileUtil.java:729-759), reachable from InstallationController.extractFilesFromPEARFile/installComponent (uimaj-core/.../pear/tools/InstallationController.java:722-796, 1555-1563), PackageInstaller.installPackage, and PMController.extractInputPears (uimaj-tools/.../pear/merger/PMController.java:357-364); a malicious PEAR/JAR entry name such as ../../x yields arbitrary file write as the installing user. It is credible and unfixed, but I did not select it as the single candidate because the deserialization weakness is more central (core load APIs + network transport) and typically yields code execution rather than a file-write primitive.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible and source-supported but not chosen for the one-candidate slot; also requires the operator to install/merge an untrusted PEAR, whereas the deserialization sinks are on documented load/RPC paths.

rejected_leads.lead: jVinci XTalk parser robustness: negative/oversized lengths from the network (int utflen = readInt; only an upper bound is checked) and unbounded element recursion/array indexing (childrenCount[6969]) can produce NegativeArraySizeException, OOM or StackOverflowError (jVinci/.../XTalkTransporter.java:361-380, 422-430; document/XMLToXTalk.java:80-135).
rejected_leads.reason: Denial-of-service only and largely uncaught-exception behavior; weaker impact and evidence than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Optional XML hardening escape hatch: setting the system property uima.xml.enable.doctype_decl=true suppresses DISALLOW_DOCTYPE_DECL in XMLUtils.createSAXParserFactory/createDocumentBuilderFactory while external-general-entities is not disabled, potentially re-enabling XXE/entity expansion (uimaj-core/.../internal/util/XMLUtils.java:61-73, 563-595, 673-695).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires an administrator to explicitly opt in (documented default is off); configuration-dependent hardening gap, not a default vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Command-string construction for locally deployed Vinci services: VinciCasProcessorDeployer builds '/bin/sh -c "..."' by concatenating descriptor command line, log dir and casProcessorConfig.getName() (uimaj-cpe/.../deployer/vinci/VinciCasProcessorDeployer.java:487-590).
rejected_leads.reason: Inputs derive from the CPE deployment descriptor, which is trusted configuration; no external attacker-controlled source identified.

rejected_leads.lead: Predictable temporary directory under java.io.tmpdir/user.name with mkdir() in the annotation viewer (uimaj-tools/.../docanalyzer/AnnotationViewerDialog.java:860-863; FileUtils.createTempDir uses java.util.Random at uimaj-core/.../util/FileUtils.java:288-301).
rejected_leads.reason: Local, race/symlink-style weakness in a desktop tool; lower severity and no attacker-controlled data flow.

summary: Apache UIMA Java SDK 3.3.0 snapshot (main sources only; ~1,860 visible files, index partial). I traced the highest-impact issue to unfiltered Java-native deserialization of attacker-controlled CAS/binary data. UIMA supports Java-serialized CAS forms (SerialFormat.SERIALIZED/SERIALIZED_TSI, embedded TSI in binary forms) and loads them with plain ObjectInputStream.readObject() with no ObjectInputFilter/class allowlist, auto-detecting the format from the input bytes and exposing URL/stream load APIs (uimaj-core), and the Vinci binary analysis-engine transport serializes CAS objects over the network with the same generic helper and no authentication (uimaj-adapter-vinci). A secondary concrete issue is a Zip Slip-style path traversal in PEAR/JAR extraction (uimaj-core pear FileUtil); I did not submit it as the single candidate because the deserialization weakness is more central and yields code execution, but it is a credible unfixed lead.
